1. The animation shows how inflation wears down what a fixed income can buy. Three illustrative retirees each start with the same 10 "crates" of goods. The retirees are Edna (Jan 1949), Ruth (Aug 2006) and Carl (Jan 1966). Each one's retirement begins in a different period of US consumer prices (CPI-U).

2. The number of crates each retiree can still afford shrinks as the years pass. The bars start out full and then darken from the right. By year 20, with the same 2% raise for all three, Edna still has 10 crates. Ruth has about 9 and Carl has about 4.

3. The same income and the same raise can keep its buying power or lose most of it, depending on when you retire. Edna's period had mild inflation, so her purchasing power held. Carl's period (starting 1966) had high inflation, so his purchasing power fell by more than half. The footer says this is US history, not a forecast.

4. The animation doesn't say what to do, but a viewer in my position (64, comparing two annuity payouts) could take this away: a fixed or low-growth payout is exposed to inflation risk, so it may be worth weighing a payout with inflation adjustments against a higher flat one. A 2% raise is not guaranteed to keep up with prices.

5. That advice is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the outcomes for the three retirees. It labels them illustrative and gives no recommendation about annuities or payout options.
